title: Our strength is forgiveness
hookLine: a feast for an army from one cow, and a father's word: forgive
tomorrow: an axe meets a bow on the road. who steps aside?

cards: The smell of a big family meal reaches you before you're through the door. Now put that meal in a forest hut.

King Kartavirya Arjuna stops at Jamadagni's ashram with his whole army, and the sage feeds every one of them, a feast fit for a palace, from one wondrous cow that gives whatever is needed. The king wants her.
When the sage won't give her up, the king's men take her by force, calf and all. Parashurama comes home to an empty stall.

teach.b: He picks up his axe, goes after the king, kills him in battle, and brings the cow and her calf home. He's done what a warrior would do. And his father isn't pleased.

In the Bhagavata, Jamadagni tells his son that the strength of people like them is forgiveness, kshama, and that killing a king is a grave wrong. He sends him away on pilgrimage to make amends. Parashurama goes.
That should be the end. It isn't. While he's away, the dead king's sons come to the ashram and kill Jamadagni.
When Parashurama comes home and finds his father, his anger has no limit. He takes up the axe against the warrior kings, and the Purana says he swept them from the earth again and again.
Then, when it's over, he does something unexpected: he gives the whole earth away to the priests and goes to live in peace on a mountain. Hold the two side by side, the way you'd hold two tastes.
The father's word, kshama, gentle and hard to keep. The son's war, which burned until there was nothing left to burn.

Kshama is no small virtue in Hinduism: in the Gita, Krishna counts it among the divine qualities, beside vigor and steadiness. Many teachers read the war as what anger does once forgiveness is set down.

how: Some traditions on India's western coast tell that Parashurama won land back from the sea with a throw of his axe, and Kerala's old stories remember him that way.

o: Rama with the axe, a sage's son who fought a king
the mountain where a sage goes to live in peace
the king who took the sage's wondrous cow away

games.q: the feast and the axe — tap the pairs.
p: the king who takes the cow

s: Jamadagni praises his son for winning the cow back
he tells him their strength is forgiveness and sends him on pilgrimage.
after the war, Parashurama gives the earth away
to the priests, and goes to live in peace on a mountain.
the war is what Jamadagni taught his son
the father's word was forgive; the war came after the father was killed.

games.q: your cousin says forgiving someone who hurt you on purpose is weak. what would Jamadagni say?
o: forgiveness is our strength; he said it right after his son had won.
he'd agree; that's why his son went to war.
forgive only after they apologize; that's the rule he gave.
games.why: Jamadagni called kshama the strength of people like them, and the Gita counts it among the divine qualities. the war came when it was set down.

practice: If you have something to drink nearby, take one small sip and hold it in your mouth a moment before you swallow; notice the taste fully, then let it go. If not, breathe in through your nose and notice whatever scent is in the room.
Let each breath out be a little longer than the breath in.

wordCard.voice: Parashurama: the sage's son with the axe, told by his father that their strength is forgiveness, who fought anyway, then gave the earth away.

orig.note: Sanskrit: forgiveness, patience. Jamadagni names it as the strength of people like them.

carryVoice: For the road: kshama, forgiveness is strength. Parashurama won the cow back and heard his father say so. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.15–9.16 (Kartavirya Arjuna and the cow; Jamadagni's rebuke and the pilgrimage; Jamadagni killed; the war; the earth given away; the mountain)
Bhagavad Gita 16.1–3 (the divine qualities, among them forgiveness, kshama)
